title: Explicit FH(ℚ) lattices with prescribed torsion
question: Fowler's arithmetic FH(\mathbb Q) lattices are built from anisotropic quaternion algebras over number fields. If I want an explicit cocompact lattice whose torsion is exactly the cyclic group of order 5 (or order n in general), how should I choose the field and order, and why does this construction still land in FH(\mathbb Q) even though the resulting quotient is only an orbicomplex?
answer: Pick a number field F containing the desired cyclic group of roots of unity \mu_n(F). For example, take F=\mathbb Q(\zeta_5) and let B be the unique quaternion algebra over F that ramifies at every real place (there are none here) and at a pair of finite places so that B is a division algebra. Let \mathcal O\subset B be a maximal order and set \Gamma=\mathcal O^{1} (norm-one elements). The embedding B\otimes_{F,\sigma}\mathbb R\cong \mathbf H gives a homomorphism \Gamma\hookrightarrow G=\operatorname{SU}(2)^r, whose projection to one factor yields a uniform lattice.\n\nThe torsion of \Gamma consists of the units of \mathcal O, and these units map onto \mu_n(F). By choosing F with prescribed roots of unity one realizes exactly those torsion orders. The action on the associated symmetric space satisfies Fowler's Euler-vanishing hypothesis because every fixed-point set is contractible and has zero reduced Euler characteristic. Hence \Gamma\in FH(\mathbb Q), producing a finite rational orbicomplex even though the torsion prevents a manifold quotient.

nodes.text: torsion obstructs manifold quotients but not FH(\mathbb Q)
